Plaudits means enthusiastic praise, admiration, or approval that someone receives — usually from many people — for something they have done well.

When someone receives plaudits, people are not just saying "good job" politely. They are genuinely impressed and expressing strong appreciation. Think of the feeling in a stadium when a footballer scores a brilliant goal and the entire crowd erupts. That outpouring of admiration and approval — whether it's cheering, clapping, or public recognition — is what plaudits captures.

An important thing to know: plaudits is almost always used in its plural form. You will rarely (almost never) hear someone say "a plaudit." The word naturally comes in plural, like "scissors" or "trousers." So you say:

  • "She received plaudits for her performance." ✅
  • "She received a plaudit for her performance." ❌ (sounds wrong and unnatural)
Who Gives Plaudits? Who Receives Them?

Who gives plaudits:
Plaudits typically come from an audience, a crowd, critics, peers, or the general public — not just one person. It carries the sense that many people are impressed, not just one friend saying "nice work."

Who receives plaudits:
People who receive plaudits are usually those who have done something genuinely impressive or praiseworthy — a musician after a stunning concert, an author after publishing a celebrated book, a scientist after a breakthrough, a leader after a bold and successful decision.

Plaudits works on two levels:

  1. Literal: Actual applause — the physical act of clapping to show appreciation (this is the older, more original sense).
  2. Figurative (far more common today): Praise, recognition, or acclaim — not necessarily involving clapping at all. This is how the word is used almost all the time in modern English.

When you read "the film won plaudits from critics," it doesn't mean critics were literally clapping. It means critics praised and celebrated the film enthusiastically.

Plaudits is a formal, slightly elevated word. You won't hear it in casual everyday conversation. You're more likely to see it in:

  • Newspaper articles and journalism
  • Literary writing
  • Reviews of films, books, plays, music
  • Sports reporting
  • Political commentary
  • Professional and academic contexts

It carries a sense of weight and significance. Using "plaudits" instead of "praise" suggests the recognition is substantial and comes from a respected or wide audience — not a trivial compliment.

Here are several examples to show you how the word is used in different contexts:

  • "The young chef received widespread plaudits after her restaurant was named the best in the country."
  • "His debut novel won plaudits from critics and readers alike."
  • "The director basked in the plaudits of the audience after the curtain fell."
  • "Despite the plaudits she received, she remained humble and focused on improving her craft."
  • "The charity's work in flood-affected areas earned it plaudits from governments around the world."
  • "He craved plaudits but struggled to handle criticism."
  • "The team's performance drew plaudits even from rival supporters."
How It Differs from Similar Words

Several words are close in meaning to plaudits, but they're not identical:

Praise — The broadest and most general word. One person can praise another. Plaudits has a stronger sense of being collective and enthusiastic.

Acclaim — Very similar to plaudits. Acclaim also means enthusiastic public recognition. The two are often interchangeable. Plaudits, however, can sometimes feel slightly warmer and more celebratory, while acclaim can lean more towards formal recognition.

Accolades — Means awards, honours, or expressions of praise. Accolades often implies formal recognition (like awards or titles), while plaudits can be less formal — it can simply be enthusiastic admiration from an audience or the public, without any actual award being given.

Applause — Refers specifically to clapping. Plaudits can mean applause but most often goes beyond it, referring to the broader admiration and approval that applause represents.

Compliments — Small, personal, everyday remarks of admiration. Plaudits is much grander in scale.

You'll often see plaudits used with these words and patterns:

  • Win/earn/receive/garner plaudits — "She earned plaudits for her courage."
  • Draw plaudits — "The performance drew plaudits from all corners."
  • Widespread/universal/critical plaudits — "The book received widespread plaudits."
  • Bask in plaudits — to enjoy the praise one has received.
  • Plaudits from critics / audiences / peers / the public

• It is not a polite or lukewarm compliment. Plaudits implies real, strong admiration.
  • It is not private or quiet. Plaudits tends to be public and visible.
  • It is not given for ordinary, expected things. You receive plaudits for something that stands out.
  • It does not mean awards or trophies in itself — though awards might accompany plaudits.

If you want one sentence to hold onto: plaudits means enthusiastic, public praise and admiration, usually from many people, given to someone for something impressive they have done.

It's the kind of word that carries a sense of occasion — it belongs to moments when someone has done something genuinely worthy of celebration and the world (or at least a significant part of it) takes notice and responds with warmth and admiration.
